points.sub: Not just how, but whose and why
pts: Critical language awareness, World Englishes, and high-stakes testing ethics (Units 59, 73, 74) added a dimension largely absent from Tiers I and II.
This turn doesn't invalidate earlier practical technique — it situates it within real questions of power, access and legitimacy.
This critical awareness is itself now part of the principled eclecticism (Unit 25) an expert practitioner brings to every decision.

v: A lesson plan you have taught recently

items: Take a recent lesson plan that worked well.
Ask four critical questions: Whose English does it model? Whose languages are allowed? Whose culture appears? Who is best placed to succeed in it, and who least?
Note what the answers reveal.
Make one adjustment that keeps the lesson’s technique but widens who it serves.
Teach the adjusted lesson and note any difference.
Pairs swap plans and ask the questions of each other’s lessons.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s notes (written for this book):

lines: Lesson: a role-play ordering food in a restaurant (Unit 38).
Whose English: British menu items and phrases.
Whose culture: an expensive city restaurant; several learners have never eaten in one.
Adjustment: same functional language, but the setting becomes a highway dhaba and a college canteen; learners may plan in any language (Unit 71).

blocks.x: The technique is unchanged: preparation, role-play, feedback. The critical turn does not discard it; it situates it. That awareness is now part of the principled eclecticism (Unit 25) an expert brings to every decision.

lines: Puzzle: ‘My Class 9 learners don’t revise their drafts.’
Question: ‘Does giving coded feedback with ten minutes of in-class rewriting time increase the number of revisions learners make over four weeks?’
Evidence: count revisions in drafts before and after; a three-question learner survey.

pts: Corpus linguistics (Unit 58) gave concrete form to a principle threading back through this entire series: check assumptions against evidence.
This connects directly to Tier IV's deeper engagement with SLA research and empirical evidence more broadly.
The corpus habit, once built, changes how a teacher relates to every future claim about how language actually works.

v: Five claims about English usage; a free corpus tool

items: Collect five confident claims about English from textbooks, colleagues or social media (for example, ‘Never start a sentence with “And”’).
Predict whether each claim is true.
Check each against corpus evidence (Unit 58) or a corpus-informed dictionary.
Record what the evidence shows, including register differences.
Discuss how this changes how you respond to claims in general.
Learners bring claims their previous teachers made and check them.
Support: provide the corpus search results ready-made.
Challenge: learners explain the difference between a rule of grammar and a style preference.

blocks.x: Results (written for this book; check current corpus figures):

lines: ‘Never start a sentence with “And”.’ Evidence: sentence-initial ‘And’ appears in published fiction and journalism; less common in formal academic prose. Verdict: a style preference, not a rule.
‘“Less” is only for uncountable nouns.’ Evidence: ‘less people’ occurs in speech; ‘fewer people’ is preferred in formal writing. Verdict: register matters.

blocks.x: Corpus linguistics gave concrete form to a principle running through this book: check assumptions against evidence (Sinclair 1991). Once built, the habit changes how a teacher relates to every future claim, including claims about how languages are learned, which Part IV examines.

points.h: Language as a Global, Plural System
pts: Translanguaging (Unit 71) and World Englishes (Unit 74) both challenge a monolithic view of English as a single fixed system belonging to one group.
This connects to Unit 59's critical awareness — recognising plurality and legitimate variation is itself a critically-informed pedagogical stance.
This perspective carries directly into Tier IV's deeper sociolinguistic and research engagement.

v: Short texts showing multilingual and World Englishes use (written for this book)

items: Learners read three short texts: a WhatsApp exchange mixing English and Kannada, a Singaporean English dialogue, a formal international email.
They discuss who wrote each, for whom, and whether each is effective.
They identify what each writer knows about language beyond ‘correct English’.
Groups write a class statement: ‘What is good English?’
Display the statement and revisit it at the end of term.
Learners create a poster, ‘The Englishes of our town’, from signs, menus and messages they collect.
Support: provide questions for each text and a word bank (audience, purpose, formal, local, international).
Challenge: learners rewrite one text for a different audience.

blocks.x: A class statement (written for this book):

lines: Good English is English that works for the person you are talking to. We can use local English with friends, mix languages when everyone understands, and use clear international English for people from other places. Knowing when to use which is part of being good at English.

dek: Unit 75 of 100: three-quarters through the series. This capstone draws all of Tier III together and opens the door into Tier IV's theory and research depth.

aims.x: This unit closes Part III. Part I built classroom foundations and Part II integrated the skills through tasks, projects and communicative assessment. Part III added specialist depth: discourse and pragmatics, genre and CLIL, EAP and ESP, testing and washback, corpus evidence, critical awareness, and the teacher as researcher. This capstone asks what it means to have become an expert practitioner, and why the next step, into Part IV’s theory and research, follows naturally. Most activities are for teachers, mentors and teacher educators.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: summarize what Part III added to your practice and where it came from;
explain the critical turn and how it changes, without replacing, earlier technique;
describe the practitioner-researcher stance and its link to formal research;
trace how autonomy and assessment matured from awareness into design;
apply the habit of checking claims against evidence;
treat English as a plural, global system in planning and assessment;
place your own development within the whole series;
plan how you will use Part IV.

why: Why this matters. Tier II built integrated, methodologically grounded teaching. Tier III built genuine specialist depth — discourse, genre, autonomy, testing, critical awareness. What's left is research itself.

background.x: Expertise in teaching is not the same as experience. A teacher with twenty years in the classroom may have repeated the first year twenty times, or may have grown in each. Research on teacher learning suggests that growth depends on reflection, collaboration and engagement with ideas beyond one’s own classroom (Richards and Farrell 2005; Johnson 2009). Part III tried to provide all three.

Part III also made a shift that Part I only hinted at. Kumaravadivelu’s possibility parameter (Unit 25) asked teachers to see the social and political realities of learners’ lives. Units 59, 71, 73 and 74 took that seriously: whose English is valued, whose languages are welcome, who can sit the test. Alastair Pennycook (2001) calls this orientation critical applied linguistics. It does not replace technique; it asks what technique is for, and for whom.

A third thread was inquiry. Action research (Unit 67), mentoring and lesson study (Unit 68), corpus checking (Unit 58) and deep reflection on identity (Unit 72) all ask the teacher to gather evidence and question assumptions. Anne Burns (2010) and Dick Allwright (2003) describe forms of practitioner research that grow from classroom puzzles. Prabhu (1990) argued that what guides a teacher is a sense of plausibility; research is one way of keeping that sense alive and honest.

In India, NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 both call for teachers who are reflective, autonomous and research-engaged, and DIETs have a long-standing mandate for research as well as training (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Part IV is written for that role. It turns from ‘how’ to ‘why’: second language acquisition, teacher cognition, research methods, sociolinguistics and the ethics of new technologies.

terms.def: An approach to applied linguistics that examines questions of power, inequality and ideology in language use and language education (Pennycook 2001).
The development in applied linguistics and ELT of attention to power, identity and inequality, which situates established techniques in their social context rather than replacing them.
Teaching in which decisions are grounded in systematic research findings about what works. Critics note that classroom contexts vary, so research should inform rather than dictate practice.
A teacher who combines secure classroom skills with specialist depth and a principled understanding of theory and research, and who can explain and adapt their decisions to context.

A form of practitioner research in which teachers and learners work together to understand puzzles in their classroom life, using normal teaching activities as the means of investigation (Allwright and Hanks 2009).
The recognition that English exists in many legitimate varieties, such as Indian English, rather than as a single standard owned by native speakers.
Research that teachers carry out on their own classrooms to understand and improve practice, such as action research or exploratory practice.

A teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides classroom decisions (Prabhu 1990). Prabhu argued it matters more than any one method, and that it stays alive through reflection and engagement with ideas.
A teacher’s personal, reasoned set of beliefs about how languages are learned and how best to teach them, which guides classroom decisions and develops with experience and reflection.
